landscape: International relations has a long-standing data infrastructure. The Correlates of War project, begun in the 1960s, still supplies the backbone. Its data cover state system membership, militarized interstate disputes, national material capabilities, alliances, territorial change, intergovernmental organizations, diplomatic exchange and bilateral trade, mostly from 1816. Around this core sit competing or successor datasets built to fix its limits. They include ATOP for alliance obligations, ICB for crises, MIE and MIC for militarized events and confrontations, Gleditsch-Ward and ISD for the state system, and ICOW for territorial and other claims.

A second generation of datasets measures institutions and economic statecraft. Some cover delegated authority in international organizations (MIA, the International Authority Database), UN General Assembly ideal points and sanctions (the Global Sanctions Data Base, TIES, EU and UN sanctions data). Others cover trade agreement design (DESTA, the World Bank Deep Trade Agreements) and foreign aid from OECD donors and China (OECD CRS, AidData). Diplomacy data have expanded quickly, with embassy networks, leader travel and ambassador characteristics now available for recent decades.

The domain has 148 IR rows, plus six infrastructure tools (peacesciencer, countrycode, democracyData, states, EUGene and the Harvard Dataverse journal collections) that make dyadic and country-year panels reproducible. Many datasets are single releases tied to one article and are now frozen, while the COW components are updated irregularly. Several official sources (IMF, OECD, ICPSR) block automated access. The Voeten UN voting record was restructured in 2025, so the version most often cited differs from the current one.

core.text: The Correlates of War Militarized Interstate Disputes data (version 5.0) record threats, displays and uses of force between states from 1816 to 2014, with dispute-level, participant, dyadic and incident files. MIDs are a widely used outcome in quantitative conflict research. The coding has been revised over time, and the MIC/ICDP project recodes many cases, so findings should be checked against the alternative.

The National Material Capabilities data (version 7.0) give annual military expenditure and personnel, iron and steel production, energy consumption, and total and urban population for all states from 1816 to 2022. These components are combined into the Composite Index of National Capability (CINC), which is widely used as a control for relative power. The components are crude proxies and the composite weights them equally.

The Alliance Treaty Obligations and Provisions project (version 5.1) codes the content of written alliance agreements from 1815 to 2018: defence, offence, neutrality, non-aggression and consultation commitments and their conditions. It supersedes COW Formal Alliances for most purposes because it records what states promise, not only that they are allied.

The UN General Assembly voting data and ideal points (Bailey, Strezhnev and Voeten) estimate states' foreign-policy positions from roll-call votes since 1946, using a model that keeps estimates comparable as the agenda changes. They are widely used to measure foreign-policy alignment. In 2025 the Dataverse record was renamed to ideal points and raw votes moved to the UNGA Decision-Making Database, so replications must state the version used.

The SIPRI Military Expenditure Database reports military spending for most independent states from 1949 to 2025 in current and constant dollars and as shares of GDP and government spending, following a consistent definition of military expenditure. It is widely used as a source on defence spending. Figures for opaque states are estimates, and series are revised between releases.

choosing: Match the unit of analysis to the question before choosing a dataset: disputes (MID, MIC), events (MIE), crises (ICB), wars (COW, Reiter-Stam-Horowitz), or claims (ICOW). Many debates in the field turn on these coding choices, so report results with at least one alternative where one exists.

Build dyadic or country-year panels with peacesciencer or the states package and a single state list (COW or Gleditsch-Ward), and merge with country-code crosswalks (countrycode). Mixing state lists or code systems silently drops or duplicates observations.
gaps: Most canonical security datasets stop between 2005 and 2014 (MID, TIES, COW Diplomatic Exchange, COW Trade, IGO), leaving the most recent decade covered mainly by event-based or single-project datasets.

Data on informal diplomacy, private and covert interventions, and cyber operations depend on public reporting and are uneven across regions; non-Western diplomatic and aid activity (beyond China) is thinly covered.

Several frequently cited resources are hard to reach or changing: the IMF MONA and members' financial data sit behind sites that block scripts, SIPRI's peace operations database is temporarily offline, and the UN voting record has been restructured.
